title: Detecting Religious Language in Climate Discourse
measurement_description: The paper evaluated the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect explicit and implicit religious language in climate-related texts (sentences scraped from environmental NGO websites). It compared LLM zero-shot classification and argumentation against a rule-based hierarchical tree of religious terms to investigate how models interpret religious terms, metaphors, and ecotheological concepts (e.g., 'Mother Earth', 'sacred earth').
findings: The rule-based method consistently labeled more sentences as religious than the LLMs. LLMs struggled with implicit religious language and terms associated with nature spirituality (e.g., 'Mother Earth', 'sacred earth'), often classifying them as metaphorical or descriptive rather than functionally religious. Llama 3.3 70B classified sentences as religious more frequently than GPT-4o mini and was more sensitive to biblical references. Both models showed inconsistencies in their argumentation, revealing a bias toward explicit, conventional definitions of religion over implicit, spiritual, or postsecular ones.
